# Prompt - Ollama API

This example sends a single user prompt from Java to a locally running
[Ollama](https://ollama.com/) model through the
[ollama4j](https://github.com/ollama4j/ollama4j) client. It makes the model
name, prompt, and local endpoint explicit, then prints the assistant response.

The example deliberately uses Ollama’s API and a fixed `llama2` model name.
That keeps the interaction easy to inspect, but couples the code to Ollama and
does not provide portability, conversational memory, response validation, or
production-grade error handling. Local inference avoids sending the prompt to a
hosted model API, but it is not by itself a privacy or security guarantee.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify the local Ollama endpoint and model required by the application;
- configure a simple Ollama chat request with ollama4j;
- verify the Ollama HTTP API independently before running Java code;
- run the application with its default and command-line prompts; and
- explain why a successful response is not evidence of factual correctness or
  production readiness.

## Prerequisites and environment

Run the commands from this directory in a POSIX-compatible shell. The example
requires no API key or other environment variable. Ollama must be running on
`http://localhost:11434`, which is the default endpoint used by ollama4j, and
the `llama2` model must be present locally. Downloading the model uses several
gigabytes of disk space and network bandwidth; it does not call a paid hosted
model API.

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download)

- [`curl`](https://curl.se/)

- [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/)

## The program to inspect

`Main` takes the first command-line argument as the prompt, or uses a question
about the first Moon landing when no argument is supplied. It prints both the
exact prompt and the text returned by the model.

```java
package demo;

import java.util.Arrays;

public final class Main {

    static void main(final String[] args) {
        final String prompt = readPromptFromArgs(args);
        System.out.println("prompt> " + prompt);

        final ModelGateway gateway = ModelGateway.create();
        final String assistant = gateway.prompt(prompt);
        System.out.println("assistant> " + assistant.translateEscapes());
    }

    private static String readPromptFromArgs(final String[] args) {
        return Arrays.stream(args)
                .findFirst()
                .orElse("When did humans first land on the Moon?");
    }

    private Main() {}
}
```

`ModelGateway` creates an `OllamaChatRequest` for the fixed `llama2` model and
adds the prompt as a user message. `new Ollama()` targets the local default
endpoint. The 60-second request timeout is a workshop convenience, not a
suitable latency target or resilience policy for production code.

```java
package demo;

import io.github.ollama4j.Ollama;
import io.github.ollama4j.exceptions.OllamaException;
import io.github.ollama4j.models.chat.OllamaChatMessageRole;
import io.github.ollama4j.models.chat.OllamaChatRequest;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

final class ModelGateway {

    private final Ollama ollama;

    static ModelGateway create() {
        return new ModelGateway();
    }

    String prompt(final String prompt) {
        requireNonNull(prompt);

        final OllamaChatRequest request = OllamaChatRequest.builder()
                .withModel("llama2")
                .withMessage(OllamaChatMessageRole.USER, prompt)
                .build();

        try {
            return ollama.chat(request, null)
                    .getResponseModel()
                    .getMessage()
                    .getResponse();
        } catch (final OllamaException e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Failed to make request to the model", e);
        }
    }

    private ModelGateway() {
        ollama = new Ollama();
        ollama.setRequestTimeoutSeconds(60);
    }
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

1. Confirm whether `llama2` is already installed. A new Ollama installation
   normally returns no models.

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   After a fresh installation, no models will be listed.

   ```
   NAME    ID    SIZE    MODIFIED
   ```

2. If `llama2` is absent, download it. This is a potentially large network and
   disk operation. If you downloaded the model solely for this example, you can
   later remove it manually with `ollama rm llama2`; do not remove a model used
   by another local example.

   ```shell
   ollama pull llama2
   ```

   This process may take a few seconds to several minutes, depending on your
   internet connection.

   Once the model is downloaded, you can begin using it.

   (*Optional*) To confirm the model has been installed, list the models again:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   You should now see `llama2` in the list.

   ```
   NAME             ID              SIZE      MODIFIED
   llama2:latest    78e26419b446    3.8 GB    Less than a second ago
   ```

   To interact with the model using the command-line interface, run:

   ```shell
   ollama run llama2
   ```

   This opens a prompt where you can engage with the model. If the model has not
   yet been downloaded, Ollama will download it automatically. You can interact
   with the model via the CLI

   ```
   >>> When did humans first land on the Moon?

   Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The spacecraft carrying the astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, landed on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he stepped out of the lunar module Eagle.

   >>> /bye
   ```

   Alternatively, you can interact with the model through a graphical interface,
   such as [Open WebUI](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui), which offers
   a web-based experience similar to cloud-hosted models.

   To verify that Ollama is running and accessible on the default port `11434`,
   use:

3. Verify that the local service is reachable and that it exposes the downloaded
   model. The response is JSON containing a `models` array.

   ```shell
   curl --fail --silent --show-error 'http://localhost:11434/api/tags' | jq
   ```

   Confirm that the response lists `llama2`. If it cannot connect, start Ollama
   using the installation-specific method before continuing.

   ```json
   {
     "models": [
       {
         "name": "llama2:latest",
         "model": "llama2:latest",
         "modified_at": "2077-04-27T11:34:56.78900000Z",
         "size": 3826793677,
         "digest": "78e26419b4469263f75331927a00a0284ef6544c1975b826b15abdaef17bb962",
         "details": {
           "parent_model": "",
           "format": "gguf",
           "family": "llama",
           "families": [
             "llama"
           ],
           "parameter_size": "7B",
           "quantization_level": "Q4_0",
           "context_length": 4096,
           "embedding_length": 4096
         },
         "capabilities": [
           "completion"
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

4. Send the same style of request directly to the Ollama chat API. This isolates
   the model and service from the Java application. `stream: false` asks for one
   JSON response rather than a stream of response fragments.

   ```shell
   curl --fail --silent --show-error 'http://localhost:11434/api/chat' \
     --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     --data '{
     "model": "llama2",
     "messages": [
       {
         "role": "user",
         "content": "When did humans first land on the Moon?"
       }
     ],
     "stream": false,
     "options": {
       "temperature": 0.0
     }
   }' | jq
   ```

   Inspect `message.content` for the assistant response. Response wording and
   timings depend on the installed model build and local hardware.

   ```json
   {
     "model": "llama2",
     "created_at": "2077-04-27T11:35:14.454879153Z",
     "message": {
       "role": "assistant",
       "content": "\nHumans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The mission was launched on July 16, 1969, and the lunar module Eagle, carrying astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin \"Buzz\" Aldrin, landed on the Moon's surface at 20:17 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) on July 20. Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring \"That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind\" as he stepped out of the lunar module."
     },
     "done": true,
     "done_reason": "stop",
     "total_duration": 17505609013,
     "load_duration": 1775287777,
     "prompt_eval_count": 29,
     "prompt_eval_cached_count": 0,
     "prompt_eval_duration": 769399000,
     "eval_count": 146,
     "eval_duration": 14959001000
   }
   ```

5. Package the application. `package` compiles the code and places the
   application JAR plus runtime dependencies in `target/libs` without running
   the tagged end-to-end test, which needs the local model service.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

6. Run the application without an argument. The `prompt>` line proves which
   default prompt was sent; the `assistant>` line is the model’s response.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```

   The answer should refer to the Apollo 11 landing on 20 July 1969, but its exact
   phrasing can vary.

   ```
   prompt> When did humans first land on the Moon?
   assistant>
   Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The mission was launched on July 16, 1969, and the lunar module Eagle, carrying astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, landed on the Moon's surface at 20:17 UTC (6:17 PM EDT) on July 20. Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he stepped out of the lunar module.
   ```

7. Supply a different prompt as the first command-line argument. Compare the
   echoed prompt with the response to see the boundary between application input
   and model output.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main 'Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?'
   ```

   A suitable answer names Neil Armstrong. Treat a plausible answer as a model
   result to evaluate, not as verified evidence.

   ```
   prompt> Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
   assistant>
   The first person to walk on the Moon was Neil Armstrong, an American astronaut who was part of the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. On July 20, 1969, Armstrong stepped out of the lunar module Eagle and onto the Moon's surface, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he took his first steps. He was followed by fellow astronaut Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, who also walked on the Moon during the mission.
   ```

8. Optionally run the tagged end-to-end test while Ollama and `llama2` remain
   available. It asks a tightly constrained question and checks that the answer
   contains `Leonardo da Vinci`.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean verify
   ```

   This test is model-dependent: a failure can indicate an unavailable service,
   a changed model response, or a real application problem.

   ```
   ...
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   [INFO] BUILD SUCCESS
   [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
   ...
   ```

## Interpretation and limitations

The direct HTTP call establishes that the local Ollama service and model can
answer a chat request. The Java runs then demonstrate that ollama4j constructs a
comparable request and prints the returned text. Together, those observations
narrow a failure to either the local service/model or the Java client path.

They do not prove that every response is factual, safe, deterministic, or
suitable for a user-facing application. Model files, Ollama versions, sampling,
hardware, and provider behaviour can all change output and latency. A real
application also needs prompt-injection handling where applicable, input and
output controls, observability, retry and timeout policies, and an explicit data
handling review.
